title: Catalog — Fabric Jumpstart
summary: Fabric Jumpstart is Microsoft's new open-source catalog of pre-built, self-installing Fabric solutions — accelerators, demos, and tutorials that bundle datasets, notebooks, pipelines, and reports so a full end-to-end scenario can be deployed into a workspace with one command. This source combines the live catalog/filter taxonomy at jumpstart.fabric.microsoft.com with the official Fabric blog launch announcement and the backing microsoft/fabric-jumpstart GitHub repo (the PyPI-published Python library that actually performs the install) to capture both what the catalog offers and how the deploy mechanism works underneath. The catalog is a client-rendered (Next.js) app; catalog item listings render via client-side JavaScript, so this extraction draws on the filter/sort chrome and site metadata reachable without executing that client app, not a diff of individual catalog entries.
audience: Fabric platform teams and individual practitioners looking for a faster on-ramp than writing a scenario from scratch, plus admins/architects who want to understand the deploy-to-workspace mechanism before allowing it in a governed tenant.
why_it_matters: Jumpstart is a brand-new (2026) distribution channel for reference architectures across every Fabric workload (Data Engineering, Data Factory, Data Science, Ontology, Power BI, Real-Time Intelligence), and it changes how accelerator content reaches customers — via a versioned, CI-tested GitHub-backed package rather than ad hoc blog samples. Establishing baseline fabric-platform claims here unblocks later depth on individual Jumpstart items as they get their own sources.
takeaways: Fabric Jumpstart is an open-source, Microsoft-run catalog of ready-to-deploy Fabric solutions, browsable at jumpstart.fabric.microsoft.com and installed via the fabric-jumpstart PyPI package.

Catalog items are classified along five independent facets: Class (Core vs Community), Type (Accelerator, Demo, Tutorial), Workload (now including an Ontology workload alongside the original five), Scenario, and Difficulty — letting the same taxonomy span every Fabric workload, plus a separate time-to-complete slider and multiple sort orders for browsing.
Deployment is a single Python call inside a Fabric notebook (jumpstart.install("name")) that provisions items and can auto-upload bundled data files into a Lakehouse — no manual item-by-item setup.

The install pipeline is built on fabric-cicd (Microsoft's Fabric CI/CD tooling) and includes conflict handling — overwrite, auto-generated prefixes, or custom prefixes — for repeat or side-by-side installs.

New Jumpstarts go through an issue-first, PR-based contribution process with published design/quality standards, and every listed Jumpstart must have at least two owners on a maintained security group responsible for fixing nightly CI failures quickly.

claims.text: Fabric Jumpstart is an open-source initiative from Microsoft offering a curated library of tested accelerators, demos, and tutorials that bundle datasets, notebooks, pipelines, reports, and supporting assets for one-step deployment into a Fabric workspace.

The Jumpstart catalog filters items along five facets: Class (Core or Community), Type (Accelerator, Demo, or Tutorial), Workload (Data Engineering, Data Factory, Data Science, Ontology, Power BI, Real-Time Intelligence), Scenario (e.g. Batch Processing, Modeling, Monitoring, Streaming), and Difficulty (Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced).

Beyond the five filter facets, the catalog also offers a time-to-complete slider spanning roughly 5 to 90 minutes and multiple sort orders (featured first, most installed, newest/oldest, name A-Z/Z-A), reinforcing that Jumpstarts are meant to be quickly discoverable, fast, guided setups rather than long-form projects.

Example end-to-end scenarios Microsoft has published through Jumpstart include a real-time healthcare billing system, a stateful streaming lakehouse for industrial sales and logistics, and platform monitoring capabilities, spanning Real-Time Intelligence, lakehouse, and data engineering workloads.

Jumpstarts are installed from inside a Fabric notebook (or any Python environment with Fabric credentials) using the fabric-jumpstart PyPI package: jumpstart.list() renders the interactive catalog and jumpstart.install("<name>") deploys a chosen item, auto-detecting the current workspace when run in-notebook.

The fabric-jumpstart installer is built on top of fabric-cicd, Microsoft's Fabric CI/CD deployment tooling, meaning Jumpstart deployment reuses the same item-deployment engine as programmatic Fabric CI/CD pipelines rather than a bespoke mechanism.

If a Jumpstart's items already exist in the target workspace, the installer detects the name conflict and offers overwrite=True, an auto-generated name prefix, or a custom item_prefix, renaming item directories and rewriting internal references so a Jumpstart can be reinstalled or run side by side with a prior install without collisions.
Jumpstarts that bundle a file-upload configuration automatically upload their small sample data files into a Lakehouse's Files area as part of installation, without requiring extra install arguments.

Before a new Jumpstart is registered in the catalog, contributors can dry-run it directly from a GitHub repo and ref (tag or commit SHA) via an internal _install_from_github() call, which builds a synthetic config and runs the same install pipeline used by the published jumpstart.install() flow.

Contributing a new Jumpstart follows an issue-first workflow: open a 'New Jumpstart' issue to align scope with maintainers, then fork, branch, build against published design/quality standards, and submit a PR using Conventional Commits before the item is added to the catalog registry.

Every listed Jumpstart must be tied to a mail-enabled security group with at least two owners who are expected to remediate nightly CI build failures quickly, so broken Jumpstarts do not stay listed in the public catalog.

The fabric-jumpstart Python library requires Python 3.10 through 3.13 and access to a Microsoft Fabric workspace, and as of its 0.1.9 PyPI release was still in an early 0.x version line, having first published in January 2026 with roughly monthly point releases since.
